metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization is the share of provisioned compute doing real work over time, and it is the denominator that makes every data center efficiency claim honest.

The definition is deliberately about time rather than peak. Capacity is built for peak, but cost is incurred continuously, so the gap between what is provisioned and what is used is where money sits. An idle server still draws power, still holds licenses, and still depreciates. That makes utilization a cost metric before it is a performance metric.

For AI this matters because capacity is added in large blocks and power is the constraint. A building, its feed, and its cooling are sized for provisioned compute, not for work actually done, so idle capacity consumes the same headroom as busy capacity. The sibling concerns, stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, are the physical version of the same problem. Utilization measures whether contracted power is being converted into output, and stranded capacity measures whether the building can hold more compute at all.

What the data does not contain is any utilization figure, benchmark, or target. It also cannot distinguish idle capacity from deliberate headroom held for spikes, and a high rate can simply mean a fleet is saturated with nowhere to absorb demand. Utilization says nothing about whether the work being done is worth doing, and nothing about where the power comes from.

siblings.label: Stranded power and space per cabinet
